Amazon Purchase Spending Analysis¶

By Nilakshi Kakati

Project overview¶

This project explores recorded Amazon purchase spending during 2018–2022 using Python with the Pandas, Seaborn, and Matplotlib libraries.

The analysis examines spending over time, leading product categories, shipping destinations, and differences by respondent age and survey-reported household income.

Questions explored¶

  • How did average recorded spending per respondent change over time?
  • Which months had the highest recorded spending?
  • Which identified product categories accounted for the most spending?
  • How did median recorded spending differ by respondent age and household income?
  • Which shipping destinations accounted for the most recorded spending?

Data source¶

This project uses Open e-commerce 1.0: Five years of crowdsourced U.S. Amazon purchase histories with user demographics.

  • Dataset — Harvard Dataverse
  • Research paper — Scientific Data

Files used¶

  • amazon-purchases.csv: Purchase records, including dates, unit prices, quantities, categories, and shipping states.
  • survey.csv: Respondent characteristics and survey answers.
  • fields.csv: Definitions of the survey questions.

Purchase records and survey responses are linked using Survey ResponseID.

Analysis scope¶

The main analysis includes 1,810,793 purchase records linked to 5,026 respondents during 2018–2022. Records from 2023 and 2024 were excluded from the main comparisons because their date coverage was limited. Date coverage alone does not establish that each respondent has a complete purchase history.

Recorded spending = Purchase Price Per Unit × Quantity

Annual averages use respondents with recorded purchases in that year. Age and household-income comparisons use each respondent’s total recorded spending across 2018–2022, not annual spending.

Household income refers to income before taxes during the 12 months before the survey. Age refers to the respondent’s survey-reported age group.

Amazon accounts may be shared, so purchases linked to a respondent may include purchases by other account users.

These findings describe the respondents included in this dataset, not Amazon’s overall sales or all U.S. shoppers.

Data preparation decisions¶

  • The original dataset contains 1,850,717 purchase records from 5,027 respondents. The main analysis uses 1,810,793 records from 5,026 respondents during 2018–2022.
  • Records from 2023 extend through September 1, while 2024 contains only one record. Both years were excluded from the main comparisons.
  • Missing categories were labeled “Unknown” and retained in total spending calculations.
  • The unusually high quantities we inspected were photo-print purchases, so we retained them.
  • We identified 11,624 repeated rows in the original dataset. These were retained because no order ID was available to distinguish duplicate records from separate purchases.

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Annual spending per respondent¶

Average recorded spending per respondent increased from USD 1,286 in 2018 to USD 2,287 in 2021, before declining to USD 2,204 in 2022.

This adjusts for the number of respondents represented each year, but differences in shopper composition and purchase-history completeness remain.

Checking the yearly trend with the same respondents¶

We repeat the annual spending comparison using only respondents with recorded purchases in every year from 2018 to 2022.

This keeps the respondent group consistent across years, but does not guarantee complete purchase histories.

In [45]:
# Count distinct purchase years for each respondent
respondent_year_counts = amazon_analysis.groupby(
    "Survey ResponseID"
)["Year"].nunique()

# Select respondents with purchases in all five years
balanced_ids = respondent_year_counts[
    respondent_year_counts == 5
].index

# Count the selected respondents
len(balanced_ids)
Out[45]:
3962
In [46]:
# Keep purchase records for respondents present in all five years
amazon_balanced = amazon_analysis[
    amazon_analysis["Survey ResponseID"].isin(balanced_ids)
].copy()
In [47]:
# Calculate total spending for each year
balanced_yearly_spending = amazon_balanced.groupby(
    "Year"
)["Purchase Amount"].sum()

# Calculate average spending per respondent each year
balanced_per_respondent = balanced_yearly_spending / len(balanced_ids)

balanced_per_respondent.round(2)

Findings from the consistent respondent group¶

Among the same 3,962 respondents, average annual recorded spending rose from USD 1,357.57 in 2018 to USD 2,555.98 in 2021, before declining to USD 2,455.47 in 2022.

This matches the direction of the original trend. Changes in which respondents appear each year therefore do not fully explain it.

Having records in all five years does not guarantee complete purchase histories or establish what caused the spending changes.

Category contributions to the 2019–2020 spending increase¶

We compare category spending in 2019 and 2020 among the same 3,962 respondents to identify which categories contributed most to the recorded spending increase.

Categories contributing to the 2019–2020 increase¶

Among the same 3,962 respondents, the largest increases in identified category spending were pet food (USD 57,017.84), gift cards (USD 53,478.06), and chairs (USD 37,113.11).

Safety masks, desks, and monitors also appeared among the ten largest increases. This comparison describes changes during 2020 but does not establish their causes.

Spending labeled “Unknown” increased by USD 69,437.34—the largest increase overall. Missing category information limits our ability to explain this part of the spending change.

These are absolute dollar increases, not percentage growth.

Top purchase categories, 2018–2022¶

We now return to the full analysis sample of 5,026 respondents and rank identified categories by total recorded spending across 2018–2022.

“Unknown” is excluded from this ranking but remains included in overall spending totals.

In [52]:
# Select the top 10 categories, excluding Unknown
top_categories = category_spending.drop("Unknown").nlargest(10)
In [53]:
# Plot spending for the top 10 identified categories
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))

sns.barplot(
    x=top_categories.values,
    y=top_categories.index,
    color="steelblue"
)

plt.title("Top 10 Identified Categories by Recorded Spending, 2018–2022")
plt.xlabel("Recorded Spending (USD)")
plt.ylabel("Category")
plt.ticklabel_format(style="plain", axis="x")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Top identified purchase categories¶

ABIS_BOOK leads identified categories with USD 1.34 million in recorded spending, followed by gift cards (USD 887,639) and pet food (USD 752,842).

Purchases with unknown categories are excluded from this ranking. They account for 5.37% of total recorded spending.

These results describe purchases in the participant sample, not Amazon’s overall category sales.

Monthly spending patterns¶

  • December had the highest recorded spending within each year from 2018 to 2021. In 2022, July had the highest spending.
  • November was the second-highest spending month in all five years.
  • The number of shoppers with recorded purchases differs by year, so spending increases do not necessarily mean each shopper spent more.

Spending by shopper characteristics¶

We calculate each respondent’s total recorded spending during 2018–2022 and link it to their survey-reported age and income group.

Each respondent represents one shopper. These totals reflect available purchase records; shoppers may have different amounts of purchase history.

Recorded spending by age group¶

  • Respondents aged 45–54 had the highest median recorded spending during 2018–2022 at USD 7,450.72. Those aged 18–24 had the lowest at USD 2,762.42.
  • Group sizes varied from 155 Respondents aged 65 and older to 1,813 Respondents aged 25–34.
  • These comparisons describe this participant sample. Differences in available purchase history may affect Respondent totals, and the results do not establish that age causes spending differences.

Recorded spending by household income¶

Among respondents who reported household income, median recorded spending increased across income ranges—from USD 3,449.58 in the lowest range to USD 10,708.77 in the highest.

Income refers to household income before taxes during the 12 months before the survey. Spending totals cover 2018–2022, so the periods differ.

Recorded spending by shipping destination¶

  • California led known shipping destinations with USD 4.24 million in recorded spending, followed by Texas at USD 3.19 million and Florida at USD 2.61 million during 2018–2022.
  • The ranking excludes 85,834 purchase records with missing shipping states.
  • Higher totals may reflect more respondents or more recorded purchases shipping to a state. They do not establish higher spending per resident or stronger statewide demand.
  • Shipping destinations do not necessarily represent respondents’ home states, and one respondent may ship to multiple states.

Overall conclusions¶

This analysis examined 1,810,793 purchase records linked to 5,026 respondents during 2018–2022.

  • Yearly spending: Recorded spending peaked in 2021 at USD 11.12 million. Average recorded spending per respondent active that year also peaked at USD 2,287.14.

  • Consistent respondent check: Among the same 3,962 respondents with recorded purchases in all five years, average annual recorded spending rose from USD 1,357.57 in 2018 to USD 2,555.98 in 2021, then declined to USD 2,455.47 in 2022. Changes in respondent coverage therefore do not fully explain the original trend.

  • Category changes: Within that consistent respondent group, pet food, gift cards, and chairs had the largest identified-category spending increases between 2019 and 2020. “Unknown” had the largest increase overall, limiting how fully we can explain the change.

  • Monthly patterns: December had the highest recorded spending within each year from 2018 to 2021; July led in 2022. November ranked second in all five years.

  • Overall category ranking: Across the full analysis sample, ABIS_BOOK led identified categories with USD 1.34 million in recorded spending. Unknown categories accounted for 5.37% of spending and were excluded from this ranking.

  • Age groups: Respondents aged 45–54 had the highest median recorded spending at USD 7,450.72; those aged 18–24 had the lowest at USD 2,762.42.

  • Household income: Among respondents who reported household income, median recorded spending increased across income ranges, from USD 3,449.58 in the lowest range to USD 10,708.77 in the highest.

  • Shipping destinations: California led known shipping destinations with USD 4.24 million in recorded spending, followed by Texas at USD 3.19 million and Florida at USD 2.61 million.

Limitations¶

These findings describe the respondents included in this dataset, not Amazon’s overall sales or all U.S. shoppers.

Respondent coverage and available purchase history vary. Having recorded purchases in all five years does not guarantee a complete purchase history.

Household income refers to income before taxes during the 12 months before the survey, while spending covers 2018–2022. Survey-reported characteristics may not reflect respondents’ circumstances throughout the analysis period.

Spending is calculated as unit price multiplied by quantity. It is not a verified measure of net spending after refunds, tax, or shipping. Repeated rows were retained because no order ID was available to distinguish duplicate records from separate purchases.

Age and household-income comparisons use respondent spending totals across 2018–2022, not annual spending. These comparisons do not establish cause and effect.

Amazon accounts may be shared. Purchases linked to a respondent may include purchases made by other account users. Age describes the survey respondent, not necessarily everyone using the account.

Shipping-state comparisons exclude 85,834 purchase records with missing destinations. Shipping destinations may differ from respondents’ home states, and respondents may ship to multiple states. Higher state totals may reflect differences in respondent coverage rather than higher spending per resident or stronger statewide demand.
